title: AI Has Half a Mind
author: Ellerton, Peter
summary: Peter Ellerton argues that large language models are, in Harry Frankfurt's precise philosophical sense, bullshitters rather than liars: they are indifferent to truth rather than opposed to it, generating statistically plausible statements whose accuracy is incidental to how they are produced. He uses Ian McGilchrist's divided-hemisphere theory of cognition as an analogy, arguing that AI has been built to mirror only the left hemisphere's capacity for representation, abstraction, and categorization, without the right hemisphere's grounding in embodied, lived, at-stake experience of the world -- an LLM has 'words connected to words connected to words' but has never fallen out of a tree or held a frightened child's hand. Ellerton's most consequential move is turning this critique back on schooling itself: he argues education has spent decades building a 'manufactory model' of learning intentions, success criteria, rubrics, and standardized responses that rewards exactly the representation-manipulating cognition AI now performs faster and more cheaply than students can, mistaking the rubric for the essay and the learning intention for the act of learning. His conclusion is that the appropriate response to AI in schools is neither better detection nor better AI-efficiency training, but redirecting education's actual purpose toward judgment, context, epistemic responsibility, intellectual humility, and caring whether a claim is true -- capacities AI structurally cannot supply, and which schools should arguably have been prioritizing all along.
points: Ellerton applies Harry Frankfurt's technical distinction between lying and bullshit to argue LLMs are bullshitters: they are indifferent to truth rather than opposed to it, generating statistically plausible output regulated by 'plausibility rather than truth.'

Using Ian McGilchrist's divided-hemisphere theory, he argues AI mirrors only the left hemisphere's capacity for representation and abstraction, lacking the right hemisphere's grounding in embodied, lived experience -- 'it has never fallen out of a tree, watched somebody die, been embarrassed in front of a classroom, or held a frightened child's hand.'

He argues schools built a parallel 'manufactory model' of education -- learning intentions, success criteria, rubrics, data walls, standardized responses -- that mistakes the representation of learning (a rubric) for the thing itself (a good essay), which is precisely the kind of cognition AI now performs faster and cheaper than students.

His central claim is that decades of schooling have been organized around producing assessable representations of knowledge, which is exactly the task an LLM is now better and cheaper at than the students producing it.

His proposed response to AI in education is neither better cheating-detection nor efficiency training, but redirecting schooling toward judgment, context, epistemic responsibility, intellectual humility, and caring whether a claim is actually true.
quotes: But there is something very peculiar about this intelligence: it doesn't care whether any of it is true.

The liar is actually deeply concerned with truth. The bullshitter, however, has no concern for the truth. They will say whatever they deem useful in the moment, not caring about whether what they say is true or not. Bullshit is truth indifferent.

It has never fallen out of a tree, watched somebody die, been embarrassed in front of a classroom, or held a frightened child's hand. It only has representations of these things. Human reasoning is embodied in the world and has something at stake in it.

A rubric is not the pathway to a good essay, it captures what we value about it. A learning intention is not about the act of learning. And producing the linguistic characteristics of an argument is not necessarily reasoning.

We have spent decades designing an educational system increasingly around precisely favoring the kind of cognition that AI does best. We ask students to produce representations of knowledge that can be assessed through other representations of knowledge.
The promise might be that when it can't become human-like we will be reminded that our focus in education should always have been about helping human minds to develop and flourish.
